extracted.intended_audience: Owners/operators of stationary combustion turbine EGUs, state regulators and permitting authorities, industry stakeholders, and environmental policy and legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbine electric generating units (EGUs) under 40 CFR part 60 subparts TTTT and TTTTa, including subcategory definitions (low/intermediate/base load), BSER determinations and phased standards, applicability thresholds, exemptions, and methods for demonstrating design efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA rule review commitment (January 1, 2041)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is committing to review and, if appropriate, revise this rule by January 1, 2041. This commitment is included in the regulations promulgated with this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: significant anticipated developments (expiration of IRC 45Q 12-year tax credit, potential CO2 utilization market development, market supports for low-GHG generation, and CCS economics) may materially affect costs and operation of affected sources that have installed CCS. The EPA will monitor these developments, consult other agencies (e.g., DOE Carbon Conversion Program), and stakeholders. The review timing allows states to revise standards and for EPA to act on state revisions by early-to-mid 2040s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low load combustion turbine subcategory definition and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Low load combustion turbines (often called 'peaking units') provide reserve capacity, support grid reliability, and typically operate at or near full capacity only for short periods. They often have low annual capacity factors, low capital costs, lower efficiency, higher fuel use per MWh, higher operating costs, and are generally late in the dispatch order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important characteristics: low capital costs, ability to start quickly and rapidly ramp to full load, ability to operate at partial loads while maintaining acceptable emission rates and efficiencies. Because they operate only occasionally, capital expenses are a major factor; quick start and rapid ramping maximize revenue during peak prices and meet sudden demand shifts. In dispatch, efficient combined cycle units are typically dispatched ahead of low load turbines under steady-state conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate load combustion turbine subcategory definition and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate load (cycling or load-following) combustion turbines operate at intermediate annual capacity factors, varying generation especially during transitions between low and high demand. Both high-efficiency simple cycle turbines and flexible fast-start combined cycle turbines can serve this role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors influencing developer choice between simple cycle and combined cycle for intermediate loads: expected cycling frequency (starts/stops), predominant operating load level, expected variability over the unit's lifetime. Key characteristics include ability to start quickly and ramp, and higher efficiency than peaking units. Capital costs are higher than low load turbines but operating costs are generally lower. Operating permits often restrict annual hours for simple cycle turbines, which informs longer-term planning and dispatch decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base load combustion turbine subcategory definition and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Base load combustion turbines are designed to operate for extended periods at high loads with infrequent starts and stops; quick-start capability and low capital costs are less important than low operating costs. High-efficiency combined cycle turbines typically fill the base load role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because base load units are run for extended periods, efficiency (fuel per MWh) and low operating cost are primary design/selection criteria. Market changes (e.g., increased energy storage and renewables) may reduce base load fossil capacity factors over time, but base load classification is tied to sustained high-load operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determinations and phased standards of performance by subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: For new and reconstructed natural gas-fired combustion turbines, EPA finalized Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) determinations as follows: (1) Low load turbines: use of lower-emitting fuels is the appropriate BSER. (2) Intermediate load turbines: highly efficient simple cycle generation is the appropriate BSER. (3) Base load turbines: BSER includes two components corresponding to a two-phase standard — Phase 1 (immediate): highly efficient generation based on highly efficient combined cycle turbines; Phase 2 (compliance date January 1, 2032): use of CCS with a 90 percent capture rate along with continued highly efficient generation. Standards of performance corresponding to both BSER components apply to all new and reconstructed sources commencing construction/reconstruction after May 23, 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may refer to standards as phase 1 or phase 2 standards. Phase 1 applies immediately; phase 2 introduces numerical CCS-based standards beginning 2032 for base load units. The BSER choices reflect different operational roles and technical feasibility across subcategories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affected EGU applicability thresholds (general applicability criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered an affected EGU under the NSPS for stationary combustion turbines, the unit must: (1) be capable of combusting more than 250 MMBtu/h (260 GJ/h) of heat input of fossil fuel (alone or combined), and (2) serve a generator capable of supplying more than 25 MW net to a utility distribution system (i.e., for sale to the grid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two thresholds (heat input and net electric output to the grid) determine whether the NSPS applies. The regulation also enumerates several applicability exemptions (see separate rubric): non-fossil fuel-fired units with limited fossil heat input, CHP units with permit-limited net electric sales, turbines not physically capable of combusting natural gas, utility boilers/IGCC with prior permit limits, municipal waste combustors (subpart Eb), certain solid waste incineration units (subpart CCCC), and certain projects under development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-fossil fuel-fired EGU applicability amendment (definition of non-fossil 'deriving' and base load rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend the definition of non-fossil fuel-fired EGUs from EGUs capable of 'combusting 50 percent or more non-fossil fuel' to EGUs capable of 'deriving 50 percent or more of the heat input from non-fossil fuel at the base load rating.' The base load rating is also amended to include heat input from non-combustion sources (e.g., solar thermal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and examples: this change ensures solar thermal installations with natural gas backup burners that are limited to low annual capacity factors (e.g., ≤10%) are treated as non-fossil and avoid unnecessary reporting/recordkeeping burdens. Revising 'combusting' to 'deriving' aligns applicability with original intent to cover fossil-fired EGUs while minimizing costs to units primarily supplied by non-combustion energy. Including non-combustion sources in base load rating allows proper determination of relative fossil vs non-fossil heat input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial EGU exemption for heat derived from industrial processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend applicability to exempt EGUs where greater than 50 percent of the heat input is derived from an industrial process that does not produce any electrical or mechanical output or useful thermal output used outside the affected EGU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: including such industrial EGUs (e.g., HRSGs using high-temperature industrial exhaust) could be problematic — it can be difficult to determine useful output attributable to the EGU, the fossil fuel may have a high lb/MMBtu CO2 emissions rate making performance standards impractical, and compliance costs could discourage environmentally beneficial projects that provide additional useful output with little added environmental impact. The exemption avoids creating regulatory burdens without environmental benefit and reduces the risk of discouraging beneficial developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial EGU electric sales threshold permit requirement amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend the electric sales exemption language to delete the 'always been subject' requirement. The exemption becomes: 'annual net electric sales have never exceeded one-third of its potential electric output or 219,000 MWh, whichever is greater, and is subject to a federally enforceable permit limiting annual net electric sales to one-third or less of potential output (e.g., limiting hours to <2,920 hours annually) or limiting annual electric sales to 219,000 MWh or less.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators of existing industrial EGUs can provide evidence to the Administrator that the facility has never sold electricity above the threshold and can modify permits to limit future sales. This prevents covering industrial EGUs that never sold electricity to the grid merely because they did not 'always' have a permit restriction. Without this change, some onsite EGUs capable of selling 25 MW would be subject to existing-source requirements even if they never sold electricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design efficiency determination methods — Administrator-approved alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow alternative methods, as approved by the Administrator on a case-by-case basis, to determine design efficiency (the efficiency of converting thermal energy to useful energy output). Owners/operators may petition the Administrator in writing to use an alternate method; Administrator discretion can extend to other ASME or ISO methods and to operating data. The applicability of paragraph 60.8(b) in table 3 of subpart TTTT is changed from 'no' to 'yes' (and is 'yes' in TTTTa), allowing Administrator approval of alternatives to specified test methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: many existing EGUs lack original design efficiency documentation (due to age, ownership changes, or configuration changes), and requiring old documentation or new burdensome testing would impose compliance burden without environmental benefit. The Administrator's broad discretion permits use of contemporary standards and operating data to demonstrate design efficiency and reduces unnecessary burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and effective date for subpart TTTTa (construction/reconstruction after May 23, 2023)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 40 CFR part 60 subpart TTTTa, standards of performance apply to EGUs that commence construction or reconstruction after the date of proposal (May 23, 2023). EGUs that commenced construction after the 2015 proposal and by May 23, 2023, remain subject to the 2015 NSPS. A reconstruction is treated as creating a new source. The same applicability criteria (250 MMBtu/h and >25 MW) are finalized for subpart TTTTa, with listed exemptions (capable of deriving ≥50% heat from non-fossil at base load with permit-limited fossil CF ≤10%; CHP units with permit limits; serving a generator with combined units effective generation ≤25 MW; municipal waste combustors subpart Eb; solid waste incineration subpart CCCC; >50% heat from certain industrial processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modification is any physical or operational change that increases emissions of a regulated pollutant. Owners/operators must determine construction/reconstruction timing relative to May 23, 2023 to know which subpart applies. The exemptions mirror those in TTTT but are specified for the post-proposal timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of combustion turbines in non-continental and non-contiguous areas
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing that only the initial BSER component (phase 1, efficiency-based) will be applicable to owners/operators of combustion turbines located in non-contiguous and non-continental areas (Alaska, Hawaii, Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, Puerto Rico, Northern Mariana Islands); phase-2 CCS-based numerical standards (2032) will not apply in these areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: commenters argued that conditions differ in these areas. EPA evaluated data (e.g., EIA-860) showing very limited new combustion turbine activity in Alaska/Hawaii and concluded limited impact on emissions/costs from not finalizing phase 2 in these areas. EPA retains authority to amend this decision in future rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: CHP unit net electric sales calculation and CHP-specific eligibility (elimination of 20% electrical-output restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For subpart TTTTa, EPA is finalizing the elimination of the restriction that CHP units must produce at least 20.0 percent electrical or mechanical output to qualify for the CHP-specific method for calculating net electric sales and net energy output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: CHP units with less than 20% electrical output could still meet applicability criteria; eliminating the 20% threshold ensures the CHP-specific calculation method is available regardless of the electricity fraction. The CHP calculation approach allows subtracting the purchased power of the thermal host facility when determining net electric sales (prior practice), intended to treat third-party developers and host-owned CHP units comparably. Note: preamble discussion indicates EPA identified an unintended effect in prior text where third-party CHPs might subtract host electricity use improperly; EPA proposed clarifications (text truncated in source).
